review_text: I know this prof isn't at UMD anymore, but I decided a review might be useful for anyone who sees this in her future as a professor. I get all the positive reviews saying you really just have to try and talk to her, but that's the way she was the first semester. She was incredibly nice, and completely turned it around the second semester. I am not just saying that because it wasn't an easy A anymore. After talking with her, studying from past mistakes, taking notes and going beyond to understand content, and staying engaged in lectures—all things that should allow someone to do well in a course—it was still unreasonably difficult. Sana purposefully put questions that were of high difficulty, beyond what the course content really required (based on what other professors assessed who had been teaching for many more years). Also, during lecture, she'd spend a majority of the class talking about theory and derivations that we did not really need to know, while spending relatively little time on actually going over practice problems. Over an hour and 15 minutes, we could get through what another professor would've done in 20. She refused to curve, despite the averages being around 60% or lower (or around that, it's been a semester). Additionally, though she was nice during office hours sometimes, she was not a nice person. Her TAs, who were very helpful throughout the semester in discussions and supportive whenever we needed it, she accused of helping students cheat because they weren't collecting exams quickly enough in a 100+ person class where they needed to organize exams at the same time as receiving them. She promised extra credit to offset the poor performance in Exam 2, arguing that we should earn the extra points rather than be given a curve. She told us repeatedly that this would be applied to whichever assignment category this benefitted us the most, and if that were true, I would've earned an A. She ended up saying that was too complicated and just gave us a tiny amount of extra credit (the points we earned for extra credit were divided so that the grade increase wasn't too much) in an assignment category that affected our grades much less, relatively. Overall, unprofessional, petty, and seemed much more annoyed at having to teach than wanting to. If you see this in the future and have the opportunity to take a course she teaches, you should hope that she has grown as a person. I completely understand being annoyed at students taking advantage of your kindness in the first semester that you taught, but that is not a reason to be unfair to students the next semester. The second star is for recognizing that she did at least try to support us at some times, even though she did not do well at it.

[+] Undisputable good quality [-] Not recording lectures or office hours: I think the whole idea behind this is that when people know a lecture is being recorded, they stop attending class. Although this is true, we have to see if this is a good thing or a bad thing for the students. It might be demoralizing for the professor since he might not be able to interact with a class and you could argue this is bad for the students since some students are lazy and fall behind schedule because "everything is recorded". So let's analyze this in detail: [+] Bobby provides OH "relectures" for people who missed the class. review_text: In short, Professor Aloimonos gave us a decent idea of some of the fundamental theory involved in computer vision, but when it came to coursework and projects he was pretty much uninvolved and we were on our own. If you want information about the course syllabus, you can just search up "cmsc426 prg" and you should see the Perception and Robotics Group which has links to all of the syllabi from when this course was taught. Pros: - The lectures were helpful for doing well on the midterm, and marginally helpful for the projects. I went to most of the lectures, and I would say they were better for getting a conceptual idea about certain topics. He also writes stuff on the board (equations, diagrams, derivations) that are not in the slides so I would suggest going because just reading the slides alone is pretty confusing. They did help me in some of the projects, and going to them likely boosted my score on the midterm. The professor also did some review before the midterm which was pretty helpful. The lectures also became very close-knit after a few weeks since most people didn't bother coming to them, so if you had questions it was pretty easy to ask. - The projects were at least about interesting topics in computer vision. The last project even involved using a machine learning model for a practical application, so I think they were probably the most interesting and helpful part of the course. Also, we had 8 late days total to use for the first 3 projects, so that we could get full credit even if we used a few late days. - Grading was lenient in my opinion (The professor says he "doesn't believe in grades"). The median grades for all projects besides the last one were all 100%, producing some output and writing a good report was good enough to get a good score. The midterm exam was a little difficult (median 80%). Also, we had a "participation" grade where all you had to do was say something in the Piazza at least 15 or so times, which literally everyone got full credit for. The final project had a median of 75%, that was definitely one that they graded more harshly, since your grade depended on the performance of your model. I heard the final exam was tough, but I can't speak to it since I decided to do the project instead. The overall average course grade was an A- according to the TAs. This semester, 90% was an A, 76% was a B, and 66% was a C+. - The professor is pretty nice and friendly. He is also very involved in computer vision and robotics research at UMD if that's something you are interested in. Cons: - I said the lectures were helpful, but they definitely could have been much better. The professor had a habit of skipping over some details and that could sometimes make things hard to understand. You also better remember your linear algebra or else you won't be able to follow this class. The lectures also barely covered anything about the projects, he NEVER went over any actual code, so you had to figure out how to implement the things he's saying in Python on your own. - The TAs completely ran as far as projects, exams, and grading go. We had a piazza that the professor probably was not even a part of, the TAs were responsible for responding to questions there. Sometimes they only provided clarification for projects ON THE DAY THEY WERE DUE, which was very stressful. Sometimes they would even provide conflicting information. I would highly suggest starting these projects early especially if you don't know what you are doing. Otherwise, you will struggle. - We did not have great preparation for the midterm besides the lectures and all of their slides. At the very least, the slides, our notes, and the projects were decent material to study. The TAs provided a practice midterm, which would have been helpful had they also given us the answer key. They couldn't properly answer the questions in office hours either, rendering that practice midterm basically useless. There was no practice final, however the professor covered some questions in class that he indicated would be on the final. - Grading took an extremely long time and was not organized at all. We were split onto groups in ELMS, and somehow the TAs were always confused on who was in it what group. Project 1 was due in late September but I'm pretty sure we only got our grades in early December for that one. I'm pretty sure some people didn't even get project 3 grades by the time they submitted grades to Testudo. The midterm exam was multiple choice, because according to the TAs it would be "faster to grade." It still took several weeks to grade and when we got that back, there were numerous grading errors and confusions. I'm almost positive the TAs didn't have an answer key when grading that test. After all of the regrading, my score went up by 17%. - This course barely scratches the surface of computer vision. He introduces some research in computer vision, but we are barely given any understanding of it as it is very brief in the lecture. Overall, this Professor was decent for this subject but the way he ran this class had several flaws. If you choose to take him, my suggestion is to go to lectures, take some notes, get a decent project group, and start early.

review_text: I don't usually do reviews, but I really wish someone would have warned me about this class before I took it. Rather than using structured slides, they taught freely while writing things on a Google Jamboard (essentially a virtual whiteboard). This is fine if you know exactly what you want to talk about, but unfortunately Jacobs had a tendency to make a lot of mistakes and get confused while teaching. I never retained anything from lecture until I googled things on my own to learn them. I also felt like the general flow of topics could have been a little better. 3. Responsiveness & Grading- This class had one of the worst Piazza response rates. There were times where I would have questions that went over 4 days unanswered. review_text: Course: Despite the name, this is really more 25% Objected-Oriented Programming, 75% Data Structures and Algorithms. So don't go into this course thinking it'll be more of the same stuff as CMSC131. Any of the Java you learn in this course is really taught in order to understand the ideas and implementations of the Data Structures and Algorithms you use throughout the course. Lectures: I'd say it's very important to attend lecture. Pedram records so there's really no excuse to not go through it, especially since he does a really good job highlighting how the various Data Structures and Algorithms he covers works. He even goes over many of the algorithms that you'll need to implement in the projects step by step, so attending lectures will make the projects much easier. Discussion/Lab: These were weird because they were more like a second lecture than an actual lab. These are generally miscellaneous Java topics that may or may not appear in a project/test. These are not as worth attending, with the only exception being when the TAs cover sorting algorithms. These are also recorded and you can also watch any TA's recording so if you didn't get a good TA for your section you can just watch the other TA's discussion. Projects: Most of the projects in this course focus on implementing functionality of data structures/algorithms. Again, attending lecture helps a lot with these projects. Implementing the projects is fairly easy and shouldn't take more than a day or two. The main thing is to make sure you know how to debug your code and write student tests as secret tests are usually weighted around 10-20% of the grade. Main thing I'd recommend is writing student tests as you work on the project, I felt that helped me a lot with making sure my projects were good. Also try to maintain good style and write comments as you go so you don't have to deal with doing it all at the end. Quizzes: There are 5 quizzes of varying formats. 2 of them were "write code" quizzes. When Pedram asks you to write code he expects you to know how to write an algorithm that solves a problem from scratch. The main way you can practice this is through the practice tests and projects. He recommends you write the algorithm out on paper and then code it up on Eclipse. I'd recommend knowing how to trace out algorithms, pay attention to the specific details of the question, as well as practicing material that relates to what Pedram says the quiz will focus on. Another one was a "debugging" quiz where you sat with a TA and showed them that you can use the debugger. Just know how to use the debugger and it's a free 30 points. Last 2 quizzes are take-home "project" quizzes which simply involved you having to write a code piece on Eclipse, which are also free 30 points each since there are no secret tests with these quizzes and lecture + lab gets canceled that day so you can work on those quizzes. Exams: Exams generally consist of 3 parts, Fill-In-The-Blank, Short-Answer, and Code Writing. For code writing my advice is the same as the code writing involved in the quizzes. For short-answer questions, I'd recommend knowing the slide material and knowing how to trace out any of the algorithms that you learn in class/implement in projects. Understand how the Java compiler works as that'll be important for understanding some of the concepts you need to know for these exams. For fill-in-the-blanks, again just review the slides thoroughly and use a tool like Quizlet to memorize key terms. Other Random Advice - I didn't go to office hours (didn't really need to) but if you are struggling I'd recommend it. The TA's this semester were very good and helpful. If you have small questions, use Piazza, the TA's (and even Pedram at times) will respond quite quickly. - Pay attention to Pedram's posts on Piazza, especially when he releases details about the Quizzes/Exams. He gives away a lot about what the test will focus on which will help you guide your studying. - Don't rely on the practice exams for your studying. While they offer some good material for practice they rarely if ever cover everything you'll need to go over for the test. Instead, try to create your own practice questions based on the slide material as well as study how you implemented the projects. If Pedram recommends you do a project before a test then make sure to do that project for practice. I'd also recommend practicing questions on the site Leetcode. Some of the questions are a bit advanced but the site offers good practice for questions related to certain data structures (especially LinkedList and Trees). Other Information - Exam averages in order were 66.96%, 67.05%, 78.31%. Final average was around 72%. Overall class average was 81.1% (this combines exams, quizzes, projects). Curve is unknown but I had a 96.28% and got an A+. Class Review: This was a great class and probably my favorite class this semester. Grew a real love for data structures and algorithms thanks to Pedram's teaching and the projects he gave. Exams are on the tougher side but are 100% doable if you pay attention to what Pedram posts about them and make sure to practice all the material instead of just relying on practice exams. Due to CMSC132 being a gateway class I can't say I'd 100% reccomend him if you are trying to get into the major (which has become even harder this year). If you want to ensure a good grade without putting a big effort it might be better to go with a prof like Elias Gonzalez or even Nora Burkhauser. If you have to go with Pedram though just know he isn't nearly as bad as most of the below reviews make him out to be and you'll definitely come out of this class both knowing and understanding a lot of really important material for CS.

Although you had to get at least a 2/3 on many of the challenge problems, everything was resubmittable, thus making it easy to improve upon any bad grades. The projects of this class were not like standard CS projects you'd typically face. Most of these projects required MUCH more thinking rather than physical coding. I personally spent a majority of the time on these projects thinking it out rather than typing out lines of code/debugging. You will most likely be completely lost at first when starting projects, but one you get it, its a no brainer. To get an A or B in this class, you MUST score 100% on these projects, which is daunting at first, but the ability to resubmit as well as the fact that the projects are graded mostly off of functionality and not things like secret tests makes them more bearable. There is also a group project... and lets just say you can do it individually but finding a good group really helps with it's completion. Lastly, there is a final that is 4 extra challenge problems. It is only required if you want an A or B, and isn't much more difficult than the standard challenge problems. I would say the hardest thing about this class is staying motivated. Because the deadlines are soft, it is easy to brush assignments away and let them pile up throughout the semester. I'd say 3/4ths into the semester, only about half the class had finished the FIRST project (note that by this time you should've been done with the THIRD). This will make this class BEYOND stressful for the end of semester, so if you do take this class, do yourself a favor and STAY ON TOP OF YOUR WORK. Other than that, Marsh truly is an understanding professor, and his lectures are typically helpful practice on project concepts and/or Q&A sessions regarding projects/course topics.

review_text: I really enjoyed the class content. I absolutely love Microbiology and my GTA and UTA were the GOATs. That being said, I did not really like the flipped classroom style but to each their own. I thought coming to lecture was a waste of my time because she records her lectures and completed slides with the clicker questions. I only went to class because that's how she took attendance. I could also be speaking out of bias because I did not want to have to pay for the PointSolutions clicker for just this class. However, I will say that the lecture videos are very informative and I have almost never had to open the textbook for this class unless it was to cite it for the PAKs. You don't really have to pay attention in class unless you sit in the front and want to ask questions since the clickers are graded on completion, not accuracy. There are occasional in person papers that you have to submit, but those are considered bonus points. Her exams are weird to study for because there's no focus but this semester, one of the GTAs hosted review sessions before exam 1 and exam 2 that were recorded and that helped. Exams are no longer open note or online! The final was also cumulative and in person starting this semester! Exam 3 (which is the final) is the hardest because it has an emphasis on Module 3 content but Module 3 is a very dense part of the content and it felt very rushed at the end of the semester. We definitely could have shortened module 1 content and extended module 3 a little bit. But I would say those are all excusable. The worst part of this class and why this class gets 4 stars instead of 5 stars was the busy work. I was taking an 18 credit semester this semester and there was so much busy work every week with assignments that weren't hard but would just take so much time. They weren't even integral to learning, they just felt so unnecessary in the long run. The PAKs? Not graded on accuracy. The discussion boards? Unnecessary research that could have been combined into one assignment. The research boxes? While they were interesting, I feel like they didn't help me too much because I already knew how to read articles. But nonetheless, busy work. I would be working on microbiology assignments even when I had to study for an exam. That's when you know it's too much work. It's an easy class, but if you're fine with busy work and you love microbiology, definitely take it!
